lessons.title: मित्राला (mitrālā) — the object that is a person
lessons.gloss: the object marker -ला — put on a person, left off a thing, and Marathi is strict about the difference

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: मला has been in this book since chapter sixteen, always in front of liking or knowing. The -ला inside it has a second job you have never been shown.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: a person you act on takes -ला; a thing does not

segments.text: मी मित्राला पाहतो. — mī mitrālā pāhto. — I see my friend. मी पाणी पाहतो. — mī pāṇī pāhto. — I see the water.

Read those two across. Same verb, same position, and the marker appears on one and not the other. Marathi puts -ला on a direct object when the object is animate — a person, and usually an animal — and leaves it bare when the object is a thing.

If you know Spanish this is the personal a under another name, and it behaves the same way: it is not politeness and not emphasis, it is a rule, and dropping it on a person is a mistake rather than a shade.
The stem is the usual one: मित्र becomes मित्रा-, then -ला. And now the old मला makes sense: it is मी through its oblique, with this same -ला on the end.

segments.instruction: mī pāṇī pāhto — the water is not

segments.text: Which objects take -ला? (Animate ones — people and animals.) Is leaving it off a person a shade of meaning or a mistake? (A mistake.)

lessons.title: मित्राला देतो (mitrālā deto) — giving it to somebody
lessons.gloss: the indirect object — the same -ला again, this time for the person a thing goes TO

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: मित्राला (mitrālā) पाहतो marks the person as what you look at. The same ending marks a different role entirely, and the verb decides which.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the thing stays bare, the person takes -ला

segments.text: मी मित्राला पाणी देतो. — mī mitrālā pāṇī deto. — I give water to my friend.
Three pieces, and each one is somewhere you can predict. The giver is first and bare. The receiver takes -ला. The thing given stays bare because it is not animate. The verb, as always, is last.

English has two ways to say this — give my friend water, give water to my friend — and has to choose an order. Marathi has one marker and does not care very much about the order of the two objects, because -ला already says which is which. That is the payoff of marking rather than positioning.
आणणे works the same way: मी मित्राला (mitrālā) पाणी आणतो, I bring water to my friend. Any verb of handing over takes this frame, and you already have three of them.

segments.instruction: the same sentence with āṇto — I bring it
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the same sentence with *āṇto* — I bring it]

segments.instruction: which of the two objects carries the marker — the person
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which of the two objects carries the marker — **the person**]

segments.prompt: Say that you give water to your friend, then that you bring it to him.
acceptedResponses: mī mitrālā pāṇī deto; mī mitrālā pāṇī āṇto
मी मित्राला पाणी देतो मी मित्राला पाणी आणतो

feedback.correct: Receiver marked, thing bare, verb last.
feedback.incorrect: -lā goes on the person, never on the water.

segments.text: In I give water to my friend, which noun takes -ला? (The friend.) Why does Marathi not need to fix the order of the two objects? (The marker already says which is which.)

lessons.gloss: one ending, three jobs — the experiencer, the person acted on, and the person given to
